For a function homogeneous of degree $p$, Euler's identity at a differentiable point is $\nabla F(x)^Tx=pF(x)$. Consequently the supporting-plane error at an arbitrary reference point $x_*$ is
\[
 b_{F,x_*}(x)=(p-1)F(x)+F(x_*)-\nabla F(x)^Tx_*.
\]
No minimizer assumption is needed for this algebraic identity. At reference zero it reduces to $(p-1)F(x)+F(0)$; the constant term cannot be discarded without a normalization. We use homogeneity under nonnegative dilations, $F(tx)=t^pF(x)$ for $t\ge0$, with $t^0=1$ also at $t=0$. Thus degree zero forces $F$ to be constant.

In the compact setting of this chapter, the original simplified formula is valid without assuming that the optimizer is the origin. More precisely, let $n\ge1$, let $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be finite, convex, nonnegative and homogeneous, and suppose $\{F\le b\}$ is compact with $F(z)<b$ for some $z$. Then $p>0$. Indeed, if $p\le0$, homogeneity at dilation two and midpoint convexity give
\[
 F(x)\le\tfrac12F(2x)+\tfrac12F(0)
       =2^{p-1}F(x)+\tfrac12F(0),
\]
whence $F(x)\le F(0)$. Applying midpoint convexity to $x$ and $-x$ then gives $F(x)=F(0)$ for every $x$, so the strict sublevel witness makes $\{F\le b\}=\mathbb R^n$, a contradiction.

Positive degree gives $F(0)=0$. Any optimizer $x_*$ therefore has value zero. If $x_*\ne0$, homogeneity places the unbounded ray $\{t x_*:t\ge0\}$ inside the compact sublevel, another contradiction. Thus zero is the unique optimizer and
\[
 b_F(x)=(p-1)F(x).
\]
The chapter's hypothesis $b>F_*$ supplies the strict witness by taking $z=x_*$. Outside this compact context, the positive constant function $F\equiv1$ has degree zero and intercept zero, whereas $(p-1)F=-1$; its positive sublevels are noncompact. These identities explain the breadth of the preceding sufficient classes without changing their compact-basin hypotheses.
reason: Actual arbitrary-reference formula includes minus dot(g,xStar). Compact corollary derives both p>0 and xStar=0 from any strict sublevel witness; n>=1 is explicit. The constant example is not described as a counterexample to compact-context convergence. Homogeneity convention matches PositiveDegree, including zero dilations.

\paragraph{An explicit four-piece realization.}
Let $c,d$ be the exact algebraic seed parameters of Module D, and let
\[
 F_D(u,v)=\max\{u,-u-v/8,cu+dv,v-17\}
\]
be its verified coercive four-piece objective. Define
\[
 \delta=c-16d-1>0,\qquad a=\frac{25}{4\delta}>0,
 \qquad \mathcal L(u,v)=(u,16v/5),
\]
and set
\[
 F_R(z)=aF_D(\mathcal L z)+a-1.
\]
Thus $F_R$ is the maximum of the four affine functions
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 au+a-1,\qquad a(-u-2v/5)+a-1,\\
 a(cu+16dv/5)+a-1,\qquad 16av/5-16a-1.
 \end{gathered}
\]
This definition is an explicit reconstruction for this edition, not an identification of an unspecified earlier objective. Module D's own optimizer remains $(-1,16)$.

The positivity of $\delta$ follows from the certified D parameters. Since $\mathcal L$ is invertible and $a>0$, $F_R$ is finite and convex with compact sublevels. The unique D optimizer $(-1,16)$ is carried to $(-1,5)$, and the minimum value remains $-1$. At this optimizer the first three branches have values
\[
 -1,\quad-1,\quad -1-a\delta=-29/4,
\]
so their supporting errors are exactly $0,0,25/4$.

This objective has an actual infinite unmodified full-BFGS failure run. For any fixed parameters
\[
 0<c_1\le1/3,\qquad c_1<c_2<1,
\]
let $x_k,g_k,H_k,\alpha_k$ be the verified D run. Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \widehat x_k&=\mathcal L^{-1}x_k,&
 \widehat g_k&=a\mathcal L^Tg_k,\\
 \widehat H_k&=a^{-1}\mathcal L^{-1}H_k\mathcal L^{-T},&
 \widehat\alpha_k&=\alpha_k.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The gradients are the actual derivatives of $F_R$ at the accepted points, and $\widehat H_0\succ0$. Direct substitution in the inverse-BFGS update proves that these are its exact next matrices and steps. Both the predicted and actual objective decreases and the secant curvature are multiplied by $a$, so Armijo and weak Wolfe hold with the same constants. This proves a transformed full-BFGS run, rather than prescribing an unrelated sequence of endpoint pairs.

The iterates satisfy $\widehat x_k\to0$, while their strictly decreasing values tend to $a-1>-1$; zero is nonstationary. In every three phases the actual supporting errors repeat $0,0,25/4$. The actual positive secant curvatures are $a$ times those of D and tend to zero. On the fixed band
\[
 K=\{F_R\le F_R(\widehat x_0)\},\qquad
 F_R\ge -1+a,
\]
all these accepted points remain above the band threshold. Applying (SP) to successive points with indices $3m+1$ and $3m+2$ would give $(25/4)^2\le C'T_k$ for every cycle, a contradiction as $T_k\to0$. Thus (SP), and by the compact-domain equivalence also (RS), fail on this actual initial sublevel. The construction specifies both the objective and the infinite full-BFGS trajectory.
reason: Delta is c-16d-1, not 16d-c. Failure exists for the displayed source constant range; no arbitrary-H0 failure or arbitrary-c1 claim. The SP band eta=a is fixed before the proposed constant. Transformation is actual full inverse-BFGS, not a matrix-convergence assumption.

For a certificate with a finite continuous extension to $p$, accessible incoming pairs with $t\to0$ force
\[
 W(p)(g_i-g_j)=0.
\]
Thus its range is tangential to the accessible jump directions. Visibility then requires a nonzero common tangential gradient. Algebraically,
\[
 P_Ug_i=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\aff\{g_1,\dots,g_r\}.
\]
The condition $0\in\aff G$ is weaker than $0\in\conv G$: a point can have no tangent descent of this type yet remain nonstationary for the convex objective.

This limiting picture is an interpretation under the stated continuity and accessibility qualifications, \emph{not} a proof for arbitrary fields. Proposition~\ref{G:prop:star} supplies the rigorous obstruction without those regularity assumptions. Eligibility matters: some local derivative jumps cannot be crossed by arbitrarily small steps satisfying the fixed Wolfe condition.
new:
For a certificate with a finite continuous extension to $p$, consider actual eligible incoming pairs on the fixed positive band, with both endpoints tending to $p$, $d\to0$, $t\to0$, and limiting gradient jump $j$. The secant inequality and continuity give
\[
 j^TW(p)j=0,\qquad W(p)j=0,
\]
where the second conclusion uses positive semidefiniteness. Let $N_{\rm acc}$ be the span of all such accessible limiting jumps, and set $U_{\rm acc}=N_{\rm acc}^{\perp}$. Then
\[
 \operatorname{range}W(p)\subseteq U_{\rm acc}.
\]
For a limiting gradient $g$ at which visibility persists, $g^TW(p)g>0$ implies $P_{U_{\rm acc}}g\ne0$.

This conclusion concerns the accessible span. It does not identify $N_{\rm acc}$ with the earlier space $N$ generated by all active-gradient differences. A nonzero common projection onto $U=N^\perp$ follows if the accessible jumps span $N$, or if $W(p)$ is otherwise known to annihilate all active differences. Under that additional hypothesis, the common projection is nonzero by visibility. Independently of accessibility, the following algebraic identity is exact:
\[
 P_Ug_i=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad0\in\aff\{g_1,\dots,g_r\}.
\]
The affine-hull condition is weaker than $0\in\conv\{g_1,\dots,g_r\}$ and need not imply stationarity for the convex objective.

The distinction is realized by the finite strongly convex objective
\[
 f(x)=\tfrac12(x+2)^2+|x|,
 \qquad (c_1,c_2)=(1/8,1/4).
\]
On every compact positive band, $W\equiv1$ is a transported certificate. Indeed, every eligible pair with $d\le1/4$ stays on one smooth side of zero: a right-to-left crossing contradicts weak Wolfe, and a left-to-right crossing contradicts Armijo and the small-decrease bound. Hence $f'(z)-f'(x)=z-x$, proving (S) with $C=1$; transport is equality, and the positive-band gradient bound proves visibility. Weak Wolfe gives $d\le4t/3$, so $t\to0$ eventually makes $d\le1/4$; as both endpoints tend to the same point, every accessible limiting jump is therefore zero. Nevertheless the actual limiting active gradients at zero are $1$ and $3$, so $N=\mathbb R$ and $U=\{0\}$. The full-active tangential conclusion would be false here. The later no-certificate example uses the different constants $(1/4,1/2)$ and is consistent with this distinction.

This limiting argument uses the stated finite-extension and accessibility hypotheses only in this interpretation. It is not a proof for arbitrary discontinuous or unbounded certificate fields. Proposition~\ref{G:prop:star} supplies an obstruction without either regularity hypothesis. Eligibility matters: arbitrary active-gradient jumps need not be accessible under a fixed weak-Wolfe condition.
reason: Explicit Nacc avoids false all-active inference. Counterexample is an actual objective/certificate at c2=1/4, not a bad BFGS trajectory. Finite continuous extension is not imposed on general certificates.

If $c\ne0$, the normal-gradient jump magnitude $2(1+c^Tu)$ varies with $u$ on this neighborhood. More precisely, on no open neighborhood of zero can this objective equal $S(u,v)+h(v)$ with $S$ differentiable and $h$ an arbitrary scalar function. One way to see the obstruction is to subtract values at two nearby tangential points: the scalar term cancels, while the varying jump leaves a nonzero multiple of $|v|$, contradicting differentiability at $v=0$.

The nonzero condition is needed only for this nonsplitting conclusion. When $c=0$, the objective has the explicit global decomposition
\[
 S(u,v)=\tfrac12(\|u\|^2+v^2),\qquad h(v)=|v|+r(v),
\]
with $S$ smooth. Thus the subsection's existential claim is realized by nonzero $c$, not by every allowed parameter. The spike argument still makes (RS) fail in every neighborhood of zero for all $\|c\|<1$, including the zero case.
reason: All-c convergence remains local and objective-only threshold precedes all runs. Nonadditivity is existential family scope and exact fixed-normal h(v) nonsplitting, not exclusion of arbitrary nonlinear changes of variables.

The same separation holds for every fixed ordinary pair $0<c_1<c_2<1$. Choose
\[
 \rho=\frac{1-c_1}{2c_1}>0,
 \qquad c_1(1+\rho)=\frac{1+c_1}{2}<1,
\]
and replace the new point and metric by
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 z_{\epsilon,\rho}=(u,2u^2-\rho\epsilon),\\
 H_{\epsilon,\rho}=
 \begin{pmatrix}A&-2uA\\-2uA&4u^2A+(1+\rho)\epsilon\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad0<\rho\epsilon<3u^2.
 \end{gathered}
\]
For any $A>0$, the quadratic form is
$A(w_1-2uw_2)^2+(1+\rho)\epsilon w_2^2$, so the metric is SPD. The active gradients remain $(2u,1)^T$ and $(6u,0)^T$, and direct calculation gives
\[
 -H_{\epsilon,\rho}g=z_{\epsilon,\rho}-x_\epsilon,
 \qquad d=t=(1+\rho)\epsilon,\qquad\Delta=\epsilon.
\]
Thus these are strictly Armijo--weak-Wolfe eligible unit steps. Their radial quotient is
\[
 \frac{(y^Tz_{\epsilon,\rho})^2}{t}
 =\frac{(2u^2+\rho\epsilon)^2}{(1+\rho)\epsilon}
 \longrightarrow\infty.
\]
In each neighborhood first fix a sufficiently small nonzero $u$ and the resulting positive band; then the quotient exceeds any proposed bound with arbitrarily small $d$. Hence the original (RS) condition fails even on eligible near-stalling pairs for every fixed allowed line-search pair. These metrics supply individual accepted first steps and vary with $\epsilon$; they are not a single infinite bad BFGS history. Every actual infinite admissible run still converges by the main parabolic theorem.
